title: Genetics and Heredity: DNA, Genes, Punnett Squares, and Mutations
objectives: You will describe how DNA, genes, and chromosomes are related and use base-pairing rules to write a complementary DNA strand.
You will use the terms allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, and carrier correctly.
You will complete Punnett squares to find the probability of a trait and the expected number of offspring, and work backward from offspring data to the parents' genotypes.
You will recognize incomplete dominance and codominance (including ABO blood types) and explain how they change the results of a cross.
You will identify substitution, insertion, and deletion mutations, explain their possible effects, and decide whether a mutation can be inherited.

slides.title: Genetics and Heredity: DNA, Genes, Punnett Squares, and Mutations
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Connect DNA, genes, and chromosomes, and pair DNA bases
  • Use allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous
  • Complete Punnett squares: probability and expected numbers
  • Handle incomplete dominance and codominance
  • Classify mutations and decide whether they are inherited

Plan: Warm-up → 6 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 5 of Science. Genetics shows up on almost every GED Science test, and the good news is that most genetics questions are really short probability problems with a picture called a Punnett square. Today we start with the molecule that holds the instructions, DNA, and end with how those instructions can change. By the end you will be able to take any cross the GED describes, draw the square in about twenty seconds, and answer with a fraction, a percent, a ratio, or a number of offspring.
ask: Have you ever noticed a trait that skipped a generation in your family, like red hair or a dimple? (expected answer: any example; come back to it when we teach recessive alleles)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Last Week's Body and Health Review
slides.board:
1. Which body system carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell?
  2. On a hot day you sweat, and your body cools back down. Is this negative or positive feedback?
  3. A snack has 5 g fat, 20 g carbohydrate, and 3 g protein. How many Calories? (fat 9, carb 4, protein 4 Calories per gram)
  4. Will an antibiotic cure a cold caused by a virus?
steps: 1. The circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels).
2. Negative feedback: the response (sweating) reverses the change and brings temperature back toward normal.
3. 5 × 9 = 45; 20 × 4 = 80; 3 × 4 = 12. Total: 45 + 80 + 12 = 137 Calories.
4. No. Antibiotics work on bacteria. Viruses are not cells, so antibiotics do not affect them.

notes.say: These four problems review last week: body systems, feedback, nutrition math, and disease. Give the student about three minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it. Then bridge to today: every protein we talked about last week, from insulin to the antibodies your immune system makes, is built from instructions stored in DNA. Today we learn how those instructions are stored and passed down.
ask: How do you know sweating is negative feedback? (expected answer: it reverses the change; temperature goes back down toward normal)
Which number goes with fat: 4 or 9? (expected answer: 9 Calories per gram)
notes.answer: 1. Circulatory system. 2. Negative feedback. 3. 137 Calories. 4. No; antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses.
notes.watch: On problem 3, students often multiply every gram amount by 4 or forget the 9 for fat. Have them write 4-4-9 at the top of the paper first.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: DNA, Genes, and Chromosomes
slides.board:
Base-pairing rule: A pairs with T. C pairs with G.

  • DNA: the instruction molecule; a twisted ladder (double helix). Each rung is a pair of bases.
  • Gene: a section of DNA that codes for one protein.
  • Chromosome: one long, coiled DNA molecule with many genes.

base < gene < chromosome < nucleus < cell

Human body cells: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Egg or sperm: 23.

notes.say: DNA is the instruction book for a living thing. Picture a twisted ladder: the sides are the backbone, and each rung is a pair of bases. There are only four bases, A, T, C, and G, and the pairing rule never changes: A with T, C with G. A gene is one section of that ladder, the instructions for one protein, and proteins build and run your body, so genes shape your traits. A chromosome is one whole, very long DNA molecule, coiled up tight, carrying hundreds or thousands of genes. You have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; one of each pair came from your mother and one from your father. Pair 23 is the sex chromosomes: XX for most females, XY for most males.
ask: Which is bigger, a gene or a chromosome? (expected answer: a chromosome; it carries many genes)
Why does an egg cell have only 23 chromosomes? (expected answer: so that egg plus sperm gives 46 again)
notes.watch: Students often flip gene and chromosome. Use a book analogy: the chromosome is the book, a gene is one recipe in the book, and the bases are the letters.

slides.title: Worked Example: Write the Complementary Strand
slides.board:
One strand of DNA reads:

T A C G G A T T C

Write the complementary strand.
steps: Rule: A–T and C–G. Each base gets its partner, in the same order.
T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→T, T→A, T→A, C→G
Complementary strand: A T G C C T A A G
Check: pair your answer back. A→T, T→A, G→C… gives the original strand again. Same length: 9 bases each.

notes.say: I go one base at a time and say the partner out loud. I never skip ahead, because one slip shifts everything after it. When I finish, I check two things: the new strand is the same length, and if I pair it back, I get the original. That check takes ten seconds and catches almost every mistake.
ask: What is the partner of G? (expected answer: C)
If one strand has 4 adenines, how many thymines does the other strand have at those spots? (expected answer: 4)
notes.watch: A common error is pairing A with G and T with C (pairing the two letters that look alike in the alphabet). Have the student say "A–T, C–G" before every problem.

slides.title: We Do: Bases and Chromosomes
slides.board:
1. Write the complementary strand for G G A T C A.
  2. A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. How many are in an egg cell? In a fertilized egg?
  3. Put in order from smallest to largest: chromosome, base, cell, gene, nucleus.
steps: 1. G→C, G→C, A→T, T→A, C→G, A→T: C C T A G T.
2. Egg cell: 23 (one from each pair). Fertilized egg: 23 + 23 = 46.
3. base < gene < chromosome < nucleus < cell.

notes.say: Let's do these together. You say each partner base and I will write it. For number 2, think about why sex cells carry half: if they carried 46, a baby would have 92. For number 3, use the book analogy: letters, recipes, the book, the shelf, the library.
ask: In number 3, what does a gene do? (expected answer: holds the instructions for one protein)
notes.answer: 1. C C T A G T. 2. Egg: 23; fertilized egg: 46. 3. base, gene, chromosome, nucleus, cell.
notes.watch: In number 2, some students say an egg has 46 "because every cell has 46." Only body cells have 46; sex cells have 23.

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Alleles and the Words of Heredity
slides.board:
You have two copies of most genes, one from each parent. Versions of a gene = alleles.

GenotypeNamePhenotype
TTHomozygous dominantTall
TtHeterozygousTall
ttHomozygous recessiveShort

Dominant (capital) shows if present. Recessive (lowercase) needs two copies. Carrier = heterozygous for a recessive disorder.

notes.say: Because chromosomes come in pairs, you carry two copies of most genes, and those copies can be different versions, called alleles. A dominant allele shows its trait whenever it is there, so we write it with a capital letter. A recessive allele only shows when there are two of them, so it gets the lowercase of the same letter. The genotype is the pair of letters; the phenotype is what you can actually see or measure. Notice that TT and Tt look exactly the same. That is why two tall parents can hide a short allele and pass it on.
ask: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype? (expected answer: genotype is the letters, like Tt; phenotype is the trait you observe, like tall)
Does dominant mean more common? (expected answer: no; it only means it shows up in a heterozygous individual)
notes.watch: Students think "dominant" means "stronger" or "more common." Some dominant alleles are rare, such as the allele for extra fingers. Dominance only tells you which trait shows in a heterozygote.

slides.title: Worked Example: Genotype to Phenotype
slides.board:
In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant over white fur (b).

For each genotype, give the name and the phenotype: BB, Bb, bb.
steps: BB: two identical capital letters = homozygous dominant. Phenotype: black.
Bb: two different alleles = heterozygous. One B is enough, so phenotype: black.
bb: two identical lowercase letters = homozygous recessive. No B to cover it, so phenotype: white.
Takeaway: a black guinea pig could be BB or Bb. A white guinea pig must be bb.

notes.say: Here is the routine. Look at the two letters: same or different tells you homozygous or heterozygous. Then ask: is there at least one capital letter? If yes, the dominant trait shows. The last step is the one the GED loves: when you see the dominant phenotype, you cannot know the genotype for sure, but when you see the recessive phenotype, you know it exactly.
ask: A guinea pig is white. What is its genotype? (expected answer: bb, the only way to be white)

slides.title: We Do: Name It
slides.board:
Pea plants: yellow seeds (Y) are dominant over green seeds (y).

  1. Which of these are heterozygous? Ee   EE   Hh   hh
  2. What is the genotype of a green-seeded plant?
  3. What are the possible genotypes of a yellow-seeded plant?
  4. A person has one allele for a recessive disorder and does not have the disorder. What is the person called?
steps: 1. Ee and Hh: one capital and one lowercase letter.
2. Green is recessive, so it needs two copies: yy.
3. YY or Yy. One Y is enough for yellow.
4. A carrier (heterozygous, such as Ff).

notes.say: Your turn to lead. Tell me how you are deciding each one. For number 1, check two things: are the letters the same letter of the alphabet, and is one capital and one lowercase? For number 3, remember the takeaway from the last slide.
ask: Why is hh not heterozygous, even though it is the letter h twice? (expected answer: both alleles are the same version, so it is homozygous recessive)
notes.answer: 1. Ee and Hh. 2. yy. 3. YY or Yy. 4. A carrier.
notes.watch: On number 3, many students give only YY. Ask: "Would Yy be yellow or green?"

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Punnett Squares and Probability
slides.board:
1. Write both parents' genotypes.
  2. One parent's alleles across the top, the other's down the side.
  3. Each box: one letter from the top + one from the side (capital first).
  4. Count. Each box = 1/4 = 25%.

Expected number = probability × total offspring

Each child is a new event. Real counts come close to expected numbers.

notes.say: A Punnett square is just an organized way to list every way the alleles can combine. Each parent passes on one of its two alleles, by chance, like flipping a coin. So the four boxes are four equally likely outcomes, and each box is one fourth, or 25 percent. To get an expected number, multiply the probability by the total, the same percent math we did in Week 2. And remember that every child is a new coin flip: what happened with earlier children does not change the odds.
ask: If 3 of the 4 boxes show a trait, what is the probability as a percent? (expected answer: 75%)
If the probability is 1/4 and there are 80 offspring, how many are expected? (expected answer: 20)
notes.watch: Students sometimes put both of one parent's letters in the same box. Have them trace each box with a finger: one from the top, one from the side.

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Heterozygous Parents
slides.board:
Pea plants: tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Cross Tt × Tt.

What fraction of offspring is expected to be short? Out of 400 seeds, how many are expected to be short?
steps:
Tt
TTTTt
tTttt
Genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 short.
Short needs tt: 1 box of 4 = 1/4 = 25%.
Expected short = 1/4 × 400 = 100 plants. (Tall: 3/4 × 400 = 300.)

notes.say: Watch every step. I put T and t across the top and T and t down the side, then fill each box with one letter from the column and one from the row. Now I count: one box is tt, so the chance of short is one in four. The last step turns the probability into a number: one fourth of 400 is 100. Notice that the genotype ratio is 1 to 2 to 1 but the phenotype ratio is 3 to 1, because TT and Tt look the same.
ask: What percent of these offspring are heterozygous? (expected answer: 2 of 4 boxes = 50%)
notes.watch: When the ratio is 3 : 1, some students write the probability of short as 1/3. Add the parts: 3 + 1 = 4, so short is 1/4.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Test Cross
slides.board:
A breeder has a black guinea pig (BB or Bb?). She crosses it with a white one (bb).

What results would tell her the black parent's genotype? In a litter of 12 from Bb × bb, how many white pups are expected?
steps: If black parent is BB: every box is Bb → 100% black.

If black parent is Bb:
Bb
bBbbb
bBbbb
2 Bb : 2 bb → 50% black, 50% white.
Even one white pup (bb) means the black parent must carry b, so it is Bb.
Expected white in 12 pups: 1/2 × 12 = 6.

notes.say: This is called a test cross, and it is a favorite on the GED. You cannot tell BB from Bb by looking, so you cross the mystery animal with a white one, which can only give b. If the mystery parent is BB, every pup gets a B and is black. If it is Bb, about half the pups are white. One white pup settles it, because a white pup needs a b from each parent.
ask: The litter is 8 black pups and 0 white. Can she be completely sure the parent is BB? (expected answer: not completely, but very likely; with Bb, eight black in a row is unlikely)

slides.title: We Do: Squares, Percents, and Numbers
slides.board:
1. Pea seeds: round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r). Cross Rr × rr. What percent of offspring are expected to be wrinkled? Out of 60 seeds, how many?
  2. Cystic fibrosis is recessive (f). Two carriers (Ff × Ff) have three children without the disorder. What is the chance their fourth child has it?
steps:
1.
Rr
rRrrr
rRrrr
Wrinkled (rr): 2 of 4 = 50%. Expected: 0.50 × 60 = 30 seeds.

2.
Ff
FFFFf
fFfff
ff: 1 of 4 = 25%.
Earlier children do not change the odds. The fourth child's chance is still 25%.

notes.say: Let's build both squares together. You tell me what goes across the top and down the side, then I fill the boxes as you call them out. Number 2 has a trap: it feels like after three healthy children the family is due for an affected one. Probability does not work that way; each child is a new event.
ask: In number 2, what is the chance a child is a carrier? (expected answer: 2 of 4 = 50%)
notes.answer: 1. 50% wrinkled; 30 of 60 seeds. 2. 25%. Each child is a separate event.
notes.watch: The "due for it" error: some students say 100% or a higher number for the fourth child. Compare to coin flips: after three heads, the next flip is still 50/50.

slides.title: Your Turn: Punnett Squares
slides.board:
Pea plants: yellow seeds (Y) dominant over green (y); purple flowers (P) dominant over white (p); tall (T) dominant over short (t).

  1. Cross Yy × yy. Probability of green seeds?
  2. Cross TT × tt. Percent tall? Genotype of every offspring?
  3. Cross Pp × Pp and plant 240 seeds. How many are expected to have purple flowers?
steps: 1. Boxes: Yy, Yy, yy, yy. Green = 2/4 = 1/2 = 50%.
2. Every box is Tt: 100% tall, all Tt (heterozygous).
3. Purple = PP, Pp, Pp = 3/4. Expected: 3/4 × 240 = 180 seeds.

notes.say: These are yours, three minutes, and draw every square even if it feels easy. Tell me your answers and how you got them. I will reveal only after you commit.
notes.watch: On number 3, watch for 60 (that is the white count, 1/4 × 240) or 120 (half). Ask: "Which boxes are purple?"

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Read the Ratio, Work Backward
slides.board:
Offspring you seeLikely parents
All dominantAt least one parent homozygous dominant (TT × any)
About 3 : 1Both heterozygous (Tt × Tt)
About 1 : 1Heterozygous × homozygous recessive (Tt × tt)
All recessiveBoth homozygous recessive (tt × tt)

Ratio to fraction: add the parts. 3 : 1 → 3/4 and 1/4.

notes.say: The GED often gives you the offspring and asks for the parents. Memorize the four patterns in this table, or better, understand them: a 3 to 1 split only happens when both parents can pass on the recessive allele and both also have the dominant one. A 1 to 1 split is the test-cross pattern. Real data will not match exactly, so reduce the counts to the closest simple ratio. And whenever you turn a ratio into a fraction, add the parts to get the bottom number.
ask: A cross gives 52 tall and 48 short. Which pattern is it closest to? (expected answer: 1 : 1, so Tt × tt)
notes.watch: Students try to match the exact numbers. Remind them that real results only come close to expected ratios, the way 100 coin flips rarely give exactly 50 heads.

slides.title: Worked Example: Find the Parents
slides.board:
Two black guinea pigs have 48 offspring over several litters: 36 black and 12 white. Black (B) is dominant over white (b).

What are the parents' most likely genotypes?
steps: Simplify the ratio: 36 : 12. Divide both by 12 → 3 : 1.
White pups are bb, so each parent passed on a b. Both parents are black, so each also has a B.
Both parents are Bb. Check: Bb × Bb gives 3/4 black, 1/4 white.
Expected: 3/4 × 48 = 36 black; 1/4 × 48 = 12 white. The data match.

notes.say: I use two lines of reasoning, and they agree. First, the numbers: 36 to 12 reduces to 3 to 1, the both-heterozygous pattern. Second, logic: a white pup needs a b from each parent, and both parents are black, so each must be Bb. Then I check by computing the expected numbers. When two methods agree, you can choose your answer with confidence.
ask: Could one parent be BB? (expected answer: no; a BB parent always passes B, so no pup could be white)

slides.title: Big Idea 5: When the Pattern Is Different
slides.board:
• Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is a blend. Snapdragons: RR red, RW pink, WW white.
  • Codominance: both alleles show fully. Blood type: IAIB = type AB.
  • Multiple alleles: blood type has three alleles (IA, IB, i); each person carries two. IA and IB are codominant; i (type O) is recessive.
  • Many genes + environment: height, skin color. No single Punnett square.

notes.say: Not every trait follows the simple dominant-recessive rule. In incomplete dominance, neither allele fully covers the other, so the heterozygote is in between, like pink snapdragons. In codominance, both alleles show up completely and side by side; a person with type AB blood makes both the A marker and the B marker. Blood type also shows multiple alleles: there are three alleles in the population, but each person carries only two of them. A and B are codominant, and the O allele is recessive to both. Finally, many traits, like height, depend on many genes plus things like nutrition, so one Punnett square cannot predict them. The square method still works for the first two patterns; only the reading of the boxes changes.
ask: What is the difference between a blend and both showing? (expected answer: blend = in-between trait, like pink; both showing = each trait appears fully, like AB blood)
What are the genotypes for type O blood? (expected answer: only ii)
notes.watch: In incomplete dominance, students call RW "red" out of habit. Remind them there is no dominant allele here: RW is its own phenotype, so a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio is also a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio.

slides.title: Worked Example: Pink × Pink Snapdragons
slides.board:
Snapdragons show incomplete dominance: RR red, RW pink, WW white.

Cross two pink plants (RW × RW) and grow 80 seeds. How many of each color are expected?
steps:
RW
RRRRW
WRWWW
Phenotypes: 1 red (RR) : 2 pink (RW) : 1 white (WW).
Red: 1/4 × 80 = 20. Pink: 2/4 × 80 = 40. White: 1/4 × 80 = 20.
Check: 20 + 40 + 20 = 80. All seeds accounted for.

notes.say: The square is exactly the same as Tt times Tt. The difference is in how I read it. Since RW is pink, not red, I get three phenotypes instead of two. Two pink parents produce red and white offspring, which is a nice reminder that the alleles themselves never blend; they just both get partly expressed in the heterozygote.
ask: If you treated red as fully dominant, what wrong answer would you get for red-looking plants? (expected answer: 3/4 × 80 = 60)

slides.title: Worked Example: Blood Types
slides.board:
A parent with type A blood (genotype IAi) and a parent with type B blood (IBi) have a child.

What is the probability of each blood type?
steps:
IAi
IBIAIBIBi
iIAiii
Read each box: IAIB = AB (codominant); IAi = A; IBi = B; ii = O.
Each type is 1 box of 4: 25% AB, 25% A, 25% B, 25% O.
Two parents who are type A and type B can have a type O child, because each can pass on i.

notes.say: This is one of my favorite crosses because it surprises people. A type A parent and a type B parent can have a child of any of the four blood types. The type O child is just like the white guinea pig: two hidden recessive alleles, one from each parent. And the AB child shows codominance, both markers at once.
ask: Could two type O parents (ii × ii) have a type A child? (expected answer: no; neither parent has an I<sup>A</sup> allele to pass on)

slides.title: Your Turn: Patterns and Parents
slides.board:
1. Snapdragons: cross pink (RW) × white (WW). Expected phenotypes and percents?
  2. A type AB parent (IAIB) and a type O parent (ii) have a child. What blood types are possible, and how likely is each?
  3. A cross gives 14 offspring with the dominant trait and 16 with the recessive trait. Most likely parent genotypes (use H/h)?
  4. Why can't one Punnett square predict a person's adult height?
steps: 1. Boxes: RW, RW, WW, WW. 50% pink, 50% white; no red.
2. Boxes: IAi, IAi, IBi, IBi. 50% type A, 50% type B; no AB or O.
3. 14 : 16 is close to 1 : 1, so Hh × hh.
4. Height is controlled by many genes and by the environment (nutrition, health), not one gene with two alleles.

notes.say: Four minutes for these four. Draw a square for the first two. For number 3, decide which pattern from our table the numbers are closest to. Number 4 is a reasoning question; give me one or two sentences.
notes.answer: 1. 50% pink, 50% white. 2. Type A 50%, type B 50%. 3. Hh × hh (about 1 : 1). 4. Many genes plus environment control height.
notes.watch: On number 2, students often expect an AB child or an O child. Have them read every box: each one gets one allele from the AB parent and an i from the O parent.

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Mutations
slides.board:
A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence.

TypeWhat happensExample
Substitutionone base swappedTAC GGA → TAC AGA
Insertionbase addedTAC GGA → TAC CGG A
Deletionbase removedTAC GGA → TAC GA…

Causes: copying errors, UV light, X-rays, smoke, some chemicals. Effects: harmful, neutral, or helpful. Inherited only if in egg or sperm.

notes.say: A mutation is any change in the order of bases. Cells read genes three bases at a time, so the type of mutation matters. A substitution changes one base, which might change one amino acid in the protein or none at all. An insertion or deletion of one base shifts the reading of every group after it, so it usually changes many amino acids; we call that a frameshift. If exactly three bases are added or removed, the reading stays in step and the protein gains or loses just one amino acid; the most common cystic fibrosis allele is a three-base deletion like that. Mutations come from copying mistakes or from mutagens like UV light and tobacco smoke. Most important for heredity: only a mutation in an egg or sperm cell can be passed to children. A sunburn mutation in a skin cell stays with you.
ask: Which type usually does more damage, a one-base substitution or a one-base deletion? Why? (expected answer: the deletion, because it shifts the reading of all the bases after it)
Is every mutation harmful? (expected answer: no; many are neutral and some are helpful)
notes.watch: Students assume all mutations are harmful and all mutations are inherited. Use the sickle cell carrier example (protection against malaria) and the skin cell example to correct both.

slides.title: Worked Example: Name the Mutation
slides.board:
Original strand: TAC GGA TTC

(a) Mutated: TAC AGA TTC
(b) Mutated: TAC GAT TC

Name each mutation and describe its effect on how the gene is read.
steps: Compare base by base and count. (a) is still 9 bases; the 4th base changed from G to A.
(a) is a substitution. Only one three-base group changed (GGA → AGA); the rest read the same.
(b) has 8 bases; one G is missing. That is a deletion.
Read in threes: TAC GGA TTC became TAC GAT TC…. Every group after the deletion is different, a frameshift.

notes.say: Always do two things: count the bases, then compare position by position. Same length with one change means substitution. One more base means insertion; one fewer means deletion. Then I split the strand into groups of three to show why deletions are so damaging: one missing letter scrambles every word that follows, like reading THE CAT ATE as THC ATA TE.
ask: What would the strand look like with an insertion of C after TAC? (expected answer: TAC CGG ATT C; every group after it shifts)

slides.title: We Do: Can It Be Inherited?
slides.board:
1. A roofer's skin cells develop a mutation after years in the sun. Can it pass to the roofer's children?
  2. A mutation happens in a cell that makes egg cells. Can it be inherited?
  3. The sickle cell allele causes disease with two copies, but carriers are more resistant to severe malaria. Is this mutation harmful, helpful, or both?
steps: 1. No. Skin cells are body cells. The change is not in any egg or sperm, so children cannot inherit it. (It can still affect the roofer, for example by contributing to skin cancer.)
2. Yes. If an egg carrying the mutation is fertilized, every cell of the child will have it.
3. Both, depending on the genotype and the environment: harmful with two copies; helpful for carriers where malaria is common.

notes.say: Let's reason through these together. The question to ask every time is: is the mutation in a cell that becomes an egg or sperm? If not, it stays with that person. Number 3 is a great GED-style idea: whether a mutation is good or bad can depend on the environment.
ask: Why does a mutation in an egg end up in every cell of the child? (expected answer: the fertilized egg divides to make every cell in the body, copying its DNA each time)
notes.answer: 1. No; skin cells are body cells. 2. Yes; it is in a sex cell. 3. Both; harmful in two copies, helpful to carriers where malaria is common.

slides.title: Your Turn: Mutations
slides.board:
Name each mutation (original → mutated).

  1. GCA TTA → GCA ATT A
  2. CAT GAC → CAT GTC
  3. TTA GCC → TAG CC
  4. A smoker develops a mutation in a lung cell. Can her children inherit it?
steps: 1. 6 bases → 7 bases; an A was added after GCA. Insertion.
2. Same length; the 5th base changed from A to T. Substitution.
3. 6 bases → 5 bases; one T is missing. Deletion.
4. No. A lung cell is a body cell, not an egg or sperm.

notes.say: Three minutes. Count the bases first for every one, then compare position by position. Tell me the type and how you know.
notes.answer: 1. Insertion. 2. Substitution. 3. Deletion. 4. No; lung cells are body cells.
notes.watch: In number 3, students may call it a substitution because TTA became TAG. Have them count: 6 bases became 5, so something was removed.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Expected Offspring
slides.board:
In rabbits, black fur (B) is dominant over brown fur (b). Two rabbits that are both heterozygous for fur color produce 24 offspring.

How many offspring are expected to have brown fur?

A. 6
B. 12
C. 18
D. 24
steps: Square for Bb × Bb: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Brown (bb) = 1/4.
B is out. 12 is 1/2 × 24, the result for Bb × bb, not two heterozygous parents.
C is out. 18 is 3/4 × 24, the number expected to be black, not brown.
D is out. All 24 would be brown only if both parents were bb, but both carry B.
A is correct. 1/4 × 24 = 6 brown offspring.

notes.say: Here is how the GED asks it. First translate the words: both heterozygous means Bb and Bb. Draw the square, find the brown boxes, and multiply. Each wrong answer comes from a real mistake: using the wrong cross, answering for the wrong color, or ignoring the dominant allele.
ask: Which wrong answer comes from answering the opposite question? (expected answer: C, 18 is the black count)
notes.answer: A. 6. Bb × Bb gives 1/4 bb; 1/4 × 24 = 6. B uses the 1 : 1 cross, C counts black rabbits, D assumes both parents are bb.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Reasoning About a Disorder
slides.board:
Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by a recessive allele. People with PKU cannot break down a substance found in many foods. Two parents who do not have PKU have a child who has PKU.

Which statement must be true?

A. Both parents are carriers of the PKU allele.
B. The PKU allele is dominant in this family.
C. Their next child cannot have PKU.
D. Only one parent passed a PKU allele to the child.
steps: B is out. If PKU were dominant, a parent with the allele would have PKU. Neither parent has it, and the passage says the allele is recessive.
C is out. Each child is a separate event. Two carriers have a 1/4 chance with every child.
D is out. A recessive disorder needs two copies, so the child got one PKU allele from each parent.
A is correct. Each parent passed on a PKU allele but does not have PKU, so each has one normal and one PKU allele: both are carriers.

notes.say: This question has no numbers, but it is the same logic as the white guinea pig. The child shows a recessive trait, so the child has two copies, one from each parent. The parents do not show it, so each must also carry a normal allele. That makes both parents carriers. Eliminate anything that breaks the rules of recessive inheritance or forgets that each child is a new event.
ask: What is the chance their next child has PKU? (expected answer: 1/4, or 25%)
notes.answer: A. The child is homozygous recessive, so each parent gave one PKU allele; neither parent has PKU, so both are heterozygous carriers. B contradicts the passage, C ignores independent events, D forgets that a recessive disorder needs two copies.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Draw It, Then Reread the Last Line
slides.board:
1. Translate words to letters: "heterozygous" = Bb, "carrier" = Ff, "white" (recessive) = bb.

2. Draw the square on scratch paper, even if it looks easy (about 20 seconds).

3. Reread the last line: percent? fraction? ratio? genotype? phenotype? how many?

Ratio → fraction: add the parts. Wrong answers are usually the right math for the wrong question.

notes.say: This is the habit I want you to take into the test. Most genetics mistakes are not about genetics; they are about answering a different question than the one asked. So translate the words into letters, draw the square every time, and then reread the last line of the question before you choose. The GED's wrong answers are built from exactly those slips: the other color, the genotype ratio instead of the phenotype ratio, or a percent when it asked how many.
ask: A question says the ratio is 3 : 1 and asks for the fraction with the recessive trait. What do you write? (expected answer: 1/4)

slides.board:
1. DNA pairs A–T and C–G. A gene is a section of DNA; a chromosome holds many genes. Humans: 46 (23 pairs); egg/sperm: 23.
  2. Genotype = letters; phenotype = trait seen. Homozygous = same; heterozygous = different.
  3. Punnett square: each box = 25%. Expected number = probability × total.
  4. Incomplete dominance blends; codominance shows both.

Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.

Why is a deletion usually worse than a substitution? (expected answer: it shifts the reading of every group of three after it)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Why do children often look like their parents, and how can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child? Genetics, the study of how traits are passed on, answers those questions. Genetics shows up on almost every GED Science test, and most of the questions use a short routine you can learn today. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Explain how DNA, genes, and chromosomes are related, and write a complementary DNA strand.
  • Use the words allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, and heterozygous.
  • Complete Punnett squares and find probabilities and expected numbers of offspring.
  • Recognize incomplete dominance and codominance.
  • Identify types of mutations and decide whether a mutation can be inherited.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Use the hint if you get stuck.

screens.title: DNA and the base-pairing rule
screens.html:
DNA is the molecule that carries the instructions for building and running a living thing. It is shaped like a twisted ladder, called a double helix. Each rung of the ladder is a pair of bases.

There are only four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G). They always pair the same way:

A pairs with T. C pairs with G.

Because of this rule, if you know one strand of DNA, you can write the other strand, called the complementary strand. Go one base at a time, in order, and write each partner. Then check: your strand should be the same length, and pairing it back should give the original.

example.prompt: Write the complementary strand for T A C G G A.
steps: Pair each base in order: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→T.
Check: 6 bases in, 6 bases out. Pairing back gives T A C G G A.

check.prompt: One strand of DNA reads C G A T T G. Type the complementary strand (letters only, for example ACGT).

mistakes.why: You copied the original strand. Each base must be replaced by its partner: C→G, G→C, A→T, T→A.
You paired A with G and C with T. The rule is A with T and C with G, so C becomes G, G becomes C, A becomes T, and T becomes A.

check.hint: Write the partner of each base in order: A–T and C–G.
check.explain: C→G, G→C, A→T, T→A, T→A, G→C. The complementary strand is G C T A A C. Check: pairing it back gives C G A T T G.

screens.title: Genes and chromosomes
screens.html:
A gene is a section of DNA that holds the instructions for making one protein. Proteins do most of the work in your body: hemoglobin carries oxygen, insulin controls blood sugar, and enzymes digest food. Because proteins build and run the body, genes shape your traits, such as blood type or the ability to digest milk.

A chromosome is one very long DNA molecule, tightly coiled, that carries hundreds to thousands of genes. Chromosomes are found in the nucleus of the cell.

From smallest to largest:

base < gene < chromosome < nucleus < cell

Think of a cookbook: the bases are the letters, a gene is one recipe, and a chromosome is the whole book.

options: A section of DNA that holds the instructions for one protein
A long, coiled molecule that carries thousands of chromosomes
A single base, such as A or G, on one strand of DNA
A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent
why: That reverses the sizes. A chromosome carries many genes, not the other way around.
A single base is much smaller than a gene. A gene is a long section made of many bases.
A pair of chromosomes holds thousands of genes. A gene is only one section of one chromosome.
check.hint: Use the cookbook model: letters, recipe, book. Which one is the gene?
check.explain: A gene is a section of DNA with the instructions for one protein, like one recipe in a cookbook. A chromosome is the whole book (many genes), and a base is a single letter.

screens.title: Chromosome pairs and sex cells
screens.html:
Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs. You got one chromosome of each pair from your mother and one from your father. That is why you have two copies of most genes.

Sex cells (egg and sperm) are different. Each carries only one chromosome from each pair: 23. When a sperm fertilizes an egg, 23 + 23 = 46, and the new individual has the full number again.

The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes: XX in most females and XY in most males. Every egg carries an X; a sperm carries either an X or a Y.

Other species have different numbers, but the rule is the same: sex cells have half the number found in body cells.

check.prompt: A dog's body cells have 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in one dog sperm cell? Enter a whole number.

mistakes.why: 78 is the number in a body cell. A sperm cell carries only one chromosome from each pair, so it has half: 78 ÷ 2 = 39.
You doubled the number. Sex cells have half as many chromosomes as body cells, not twice as many.

check.hint: Sex cells carry one chromosome from each pair.
check.explain: Body cells have pairs; sex cells have one of each pair. 78 ÷ 2 = 39. When sperm (39) and egg (39) join, the puppy has 78 again.

screens.title: Alleles: dominant and recessive
screens.html:
The different versions of a gene are called alleles. For example, a pea plant's height gene has a tall allele and a short allele. You carry two alleles for most genes, one from each parent.

  • A dominant allele shows its trait whenever it is present. It is written with a capital letter: T for tall.
  • A recessive allele shows its trait only when there are two copies. It is written with the lowercase of the same letter: t for short.

So a plant with T and t is tall, because the dominant T covers up the t. Only a tt plant is short.

Watch out: "dominant" does not mean "stronger" or "more common." It only tells you which trait shows up when the two alleles are different.

check.prompt: In a type of plant, smooth leaves (S) are dominant over fuzzy leaves (s). Which plant has fuzzy leaves?
options: A plant with the genotype ss
A plant with the genotype Ss
A plant with the genotype SS
Any plant that has an s allele
why: Ss has one dominant S, and one dominant allele is enough to show the dominant trait. This plant has smooth leaves.
SS has two dominant alleles, so it has smooth leaves.
One s is not enough. A recessive trait shows only when there are two copies, so an Ss plant is still smooth.
check.hint: A recessive trait needs two copies of the recessive allele.
check.explain: Fuzzy is recessive, so it shows only with two copies: ss. Any plant with at least one S (SS or Ss) has smooth leaves. The tempting wrong answer, "any plant that has an s allele," forgets that one S covers up the s.

screens.title: Genotype and phenotype
screens.html:
Two words describe every organism's traits:

  • The genotype is the pair of alleles, written as letters: TT, Tt, or tt.
  • The phenotype is the trait you can observe or measure: tall, short, white fur, type A blood.
GenotypePhenotype (T = tall, t = short)
TTTall
TtTall
ttShort

Notice that two different genotypes, TT and Tt, give the same phenotype. That is why you often cannot tell an organism's genotype just by looking at it. But if an organism shows the recessive trait, you know its genotype exactly: it must be tt.

check.prompt: Sort each description into the correct category.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting a letter pair like bb under phenotype because it "means" white. The letters are always the genotype; the trait you can see (white fur) is the phenotype.
check.hint: Letters are genotypes. Traits you can see or measure are phenotypes.
check.explain: Genotypes (allele pairs written as letters): Tt, bb, IAi. Phenotypes (observable traits): white fur, round seeds, purple flowers.

screens.title: Homozygous, heterozygous, and carriers
screens.html:
Look at whether the two letters of a genotype match:

  • Homozygous: two identical alleles. TT is homozygous dominant; tt is homozygous recessive.
  • Heterozygous: two different alleles, one capital and one lowercase: Tt. (Older books call this a hybrid.)

Capital and lowercase versions of the same letter are different alleles, so Tt is heterozygous even though it uses the letter t twice.

Some disorders, such as cystic fibrosis, are caused by a recessive allele. A heterozygous person (Ff) has one allele for the disorder but does not have the disorder. This person is called a carrier. Two carriers can have a child with the disorder, because each can pass on the recessive allele.

check.prompt:
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). A man has the genotype Ff.

His genotype is {{0}}. He {{1}} cystic fibrosis, so he is called a {{2}}.

options: heterozygous
homozygous dominant
homozygous recessive
why: Homozygous dominant would be FF, two capital letters. Ff has two different alleles.
Homozygous recessive would be ff. He has one F and one f, which are different alleles.

options: does not have
has
has a mild form of
why: The disorder is recessive, so it shows only with two copies (ff). One F allele is enough for him not to have it.
With a recessive disorder, one dominant allele means the person does not have the disorder; there is no blended or mild form in this pattern.

options: carrier
mutant
phenotype
why: "Mutant" is not the term for this. A heterozygous person who has one allele for a recessive disorder is called a carrier.
A phenotype is a trait you can observe, not a name for a person. The term is carrier.

check.hint: Compare his two letters. Then remember how many copies a recessive disorder needs.
check.explain: Ff has two different alleles, so it is heterozygous. Cystic fibrosis is recessive and needs two f alleles, so he does not have the disorder. A heterozygous person with one allele for a recessive disorder is a carrier.

screens.title: Punnett squares in four steps
screens.html:
A Punnett square shows every way the parents' alleles can combine. Each parent passes on one of its two alleles, by chance, like flipping a coin.

  1. Write each parent's genotype.
  2. Put one parent's two alleles across the top and the other parent's down the side.
  3. Fill each box with one allele from its column and one from its row. Write the capital letter first.
  4. Count. Each of the 4 boxes is one equally likely outcome: 1/4 = 25%.

example.prompt: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white (p). Cross Pp × Pp. What is the probability of white flowers?
steps:
Pp
PPPPp
pPppp
White needs pp. Only 1 of the 4 boxes is pp.
1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. (Purple is 3 of 4 boxes = 75%.)
example.answer: The probability of white flowers is 1/4, or 25%.

check.prompt: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant over white fur (b). Cross Bb × bb. What percent of the offspring are expected to have white fur? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 25% is the answer for Bb × Bb. Here one parent is bb, so the boxes are Bb, Bb, bb, bb: 2 of 4 are white.
Only the bb boxes are white. The Bb boxes have a dominant B and are black. 2 of 4 boxes are bb.
75% would mean 3 of 4 boxes are bb. Draw the square: Bb, Bb, bb, bb. Only 2 of 4 are bb.

check.hint: Put B and b across the top and b and b down the side. Count the bb boxes.

screens.title: Fractions, percents, and ratios
screens.html:
The GED may ask for the same result in different forms. For Tt × Tt (3 tall boxes, 1 short box):

FormTallShort
Fraction3/41/4
Percent75%25%
Ratio (tall : short)3 : 1

A ratio compares the parts to each other. A fraction compares one part to the total. To turn a ratio into a fraction, add the parts to get the total: 3 : 1 means 3 + 1 = 4, so tall is 3/4 and short is 1/4.

Also notice the difference between a genotype ratio (1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt) and a phenotype ratio (3 tall : 1 short). Read which one the question asks for.

check.prompt: A cross is expected to give offspring in a ratio of 3 purple : 1 white. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be white?
why: You divided white by purple (1 : 3). A fraction compares a part to the total. The total is 3 + 1 = 4, so white is 1/4.
3/4 is the fraction that is purple. White is the 1 part out of 4 total.
3/1 just rewrites the ratio. A fraction of the offspring must compare one part to the total of 4.
check.hint: Add the parts of the ratio to find the total.
check.explain: Total parts: 3 + 1 = 4. White is 1 of those 4 parts, so the fraction is 1/4 (25%). The tempting 1/3 compares white to purple instead of white to the total.

screens.title: Expected numbers of offspring
screens.html:
A probability tells you what fraction of the offspring to expect. To find how many, multiply:

Expected number = probability × total number of offspring

Real results come close to the expected number but rarely match it exactly, just as 100 coin flips rarely give exactly 50 heads. The bigger the number of offspring, the closer the results usually come to the expected ratio.

example.prompt: Pp × Pp pea plants produce 120 seeds. How many are expected to grow purple flowers?
steps: Purple boxes: PP, Pp, Pp = 3 of 4 = 3/4.
example.answer: 90 seeds are expected to have purple flowers (and 30 white).

check.prompt: In pea plants, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant over green seeds (y). Two Yy plants are crossed and produce 200 seeds. How many seeds are expected to be green? Enter a whole number.

mistakes.why: 150 is the number expected to be yellow (3/4 × 200). Green needs yy, which is 1 of 4 boxes.
You gave the percent, not the number. The question asks how many of 200: 1/4 × 200 = 50.
100 is half of 200, the result for Yy × yy. For Yy × Yy, green is only 1/4.

check.hint: Find the probability of yy first, then multiply by 200.
check.explain:
Yy × Yy gives YY, Yy, Yy, yy. Green (yy) = 1/4.

1/4 × 200 = 50 seeds.

screens.title: Every child is a new event
screens.html:
Each time parents have a child, the alleles are passed on by chance all over again. Earlier children do not change the chances for the next child. This is the same as flipping a coin: after three heads in a row, the next flip is still 50% heads.

Suppose two carriers of a recessive disorder (Ff × Ff) have three children, and none has the disorder. The chance that their fourth child has the disorder is still 1/4 = 25%. The family is not "due" for an affected child, and they are not "safe" either.

A Punnett square gives the probability for each child, not a guarantee about a family. A family of four children from Ff × Ff parents could have zero, one, two, or more affected children.

check.prompt: Two parents are both carriers of a recessive disorder. Their first two children have the disorder. What is the probability that their third child will have it?
options: 25%, the same as for each earlier child
0%, because the family has already had its two affected children
50%, because two of four boxes have now been used up
100%, because the pattern of affected children will continue
why: Each child is a new event. The square does not guarantee exactly one affected child in four; it gives a 1/4 chance every time.
Boxes are not used up. Every child gets a fresh chance at all four boxes, so the probability stays 1/4.
Earlier children do not set a pattern. The alleles are passed on by chance again for each child, so the chance is still 1/4.
check.hint: Do earlier coin flips change the next flip?
check.explain: Two carriers (Ff × Ff) have a 1/4 chance of an ff child every time. Earlier children do not change the odds, so the third child's chance is 25%.

screens.title: Working backward to the parents
screens.html:
Some questions give you the offspring and ask about the parents. Two tools help.

1. Logic. An offspring showing the recessive trait (tt) got one t from each parent. So if a tall parent has a short offspring, that parent must be Tt.

2. The ratio. Simplify the counts and match the pattern:

OffspringLikely parents
All dominantAt least one parent TT
About 3 : 1Tt × Tt
About 1 : 1Tt × tt
All recessivett × tt

A test cross uses this idea: cross an organism showing the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive one. If any offspring show the recessive trait, the mystery parent is heterozygous.

check.prompt: In mice, black fur (B) is dominant over brown fur (b). A black mouse is crossed with a brown mouse. They have 22 offspring: 12 black and 10 brown. What is the genotype of the black parent?
options: Bb, because some offspring received a b allele from it
BB, because black is dominant and the parent is black
bb, because almost half of the offspring are brown
BB or Bb; the offspring do not give enough information
why: A BB parent could pass on only B, so every offspring would be black. The brown offspring rule this out.
A bb mouse would be brown, but this parent is black. Its offspring's colors cannot change its own phenotype.
The brown offspring do settle it. Each brown (bb) offspring got a b from the black parent, so that parent must carry b.
check.hint: What genotype does a brown offspring have? Where did each of its alleles come from?
check.explain: Brown offspring are bb, so each got a b from both parents. The black parent therefore has a b, and since it is black it also has a B: Bb. The 12 : 10 split is close to the 1 : 1 expected from Bb × bb. A BB parent could never produce brown offspring.

screens.title: Incomplete dominance
screens.html:
Not every gene has a dominant allele. In incomplete dominance, the heterozygous individual shows a blend, a trait in between the two homozygous traits.

Example: in snapdragon flowers, RR plants are red, WW plants are white, and RW plants are pink. (Both letters are capitals because neither allele is dominant.)

The Punnett square works the same way. Only the reading changes: every genotype has its own phenotype, so a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio is also a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio.

example.prompt: Cross two pink snapdragons (RW × RW). What are the expected phenotypes?
steps:
RW
RRRRW
WRWWW
RR = red (1 box), RW = pink (2 boxes), WW = white (1 box).
example.answer: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, or 25% red, 50% pink, 25% white.

check.prompt: In snapdragons, RR is red, RW is pink, and WW is white. A pink plant is crossed with a red plant (RW × RR), and 60 seeds are grown. How many are expected to have pink flowers? Enter a whole number.

mistakes.why: You treated red as dominant, so every plant with an R looked red or pink to you. With incomplete dominance, RR plants are red, not pink. Only the RW boxes (2 of 4) are pink.
15 is 1/4 of 60. Draw the square for RW × RR: RR, RR, RW, RW. Pink (RW) is 2 of 4 boxes, so 1/2 × 60.
50% is the probability. The question asks how many of 60 plants: 1/2 × 60 = 30.

check.hint: Draw RW × RR. Which boxes are RW?
check.explain:
RW
RRRRW
RRRRW

Pink (RW): 2 of 4 boxes = 1/2. Expected pink = 1/2 × 60 = 30 plants. The other 30 are red (RR). No white plants are possible.

screens.title: Codominance, blood types, and many-gene traits
screens.html:
In codominance, both alleles show fully; nothing is blended. Human ABO blood type is the classic example. It has three alleles: IA, IB, and i. A gene with more than two alleles in the population has multiple alleles, but each person still carries only two of them.

GenotypeBlood type
IAIA or IAiA
IBIB or IBiB
IAIBAB (both A and B markers)
iiO

IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over i.

Many other traits, such as height and skin color, are controlled by many genes and by the environment (nutrition, sunlight, health). A single Punnett square cannot predict them.

check.prompt: A parent with type AB blood (IAIB) and a parent with type O blood (ii) have a child. Which two blood types could the child have? Select two answers.
options: Type A
Type B
Type AB
Type O
why: To be AB, the child would need I<sup>A</sup> and I<sup>B</sup>. The type O parent can pass on only i, so the child gets only one of those alleles.
To be type O, the child would need ii. The AB parent has no i allele to pass on.
check.hint: Draw the square: I<sup>A</sup> and I<sup>B</sup> across the top, i and i down the side.
check.explain: The boxes are IAi, IAi, IBi, IBi. IAi is type A and IBi is type B, each 50%. The child cannot be AB (only one of IA or IB comes from the AB parent) or O (the AB parent has no i).

screens.title: Mutations: three types
screens.html:
A mutation is a change in the order of bases in DNA. Three types to know:

  • Substitution: one base is replaced by another. The strand stays the same length. (TAC GGA → TAC AGA)
  • Insertion: an extra base is added. The strand gets longer. (TAC GGA → TAC CGG A)
  • Deletion: a base is removed. The strand gets shorter. (TAC GGA → TAC GA)

To identify a mutation: first count the bases in each strand, then compare them position by position to find where they first differ.

check.prompt: A DNA strand changes from G C A T T A to G C A A T T A. What type of mutation is this?
options: An insertion, because an A was added and the strand grew to 7 bases
A substitution, because the fourth base changed from T to A
A deletion, because a T is missing from the middle of the strand
No mutation, because the strand still contains the bases A, C, G, and T
why: You compared only the fourth position. Count the bases: the strand went from 6 to 7. A substitution keeps the same length.
Both Ts are still there (positions 5 and 6 of the new strand). The strand got longer, not shorter.
A mutation is any change in the order of bases, not a missing kind of base. The order and length changed, so this is a mutation.
check.hint: Count the bases in each strand first.
check.explain: The original has 6 bases; the new strand has 7. An extra A was added after G C A, so this is an insertion. The tempting choice, a substitution at the fourth base, comes from comparing positions without counting first; every base after the insertion is shifted.

screens.title: What mutations do
screens.html:
Cells read a gene three bases at a time. Each group of three tells the cell which building block (amino acid) to add to the protein.

  • A substitution changes only one group of three. It may change one amino acid or none at all. (Once in a while, the new group is a “stop” signal that cuts the protein short.)
  • An insertion or deletion of one base shifts every group after it, a frameshift. Usually many amino acids change, and the protein often stops working.
  • If exactly three bases are inserted or deleted, the later groups stay in step: the protein simply gains or loses one amino acid. The most common cystic fibrosis allele is a three-base deletion of this kind.

Mutations come from copying errors when cells divide and from mutagens such as ultraviolet light, X-rays, tobacco smoke, and some chemicals.

A mutation can be harmful, neutral (no effect), or helpful. The sickle cell allele, a single substitution, causes disease in people with two copies, but carriers are more resistant to severe malaria.

check.prompt: A gene begins ATG CCA GTT AAC. Which mutation would most likely change the greatest number of three-base groups?
options: Deleting the first C, giving ATG CAG TTA AC
Changing the first C to T, giving ATG TCA GTT AAC
Changing the last C to G, giving ATG CCA GTT AAG
Changing the first G to A, giving ATA CCA GTT AAC
why: This is a substitution. Only the second group changed (CCA → TCA); the groups after it read the same.
This is a substitution in the last group. Only one group (AAC → AAG) changed.
This substitution changes only the first group (ATG → ATA). Every other group stays the same.
check.hint: Which kind of mutation shifts how every later group of three is read?
check.explain: Deleting a base causes a frameshift: CCA GTT AAC becomes CAG TTA AC…, so every group after the deletion changes. Each substitution changes only one group of three.

screens.title: Which mutations are inherited?
screens.html:
Your body has two kinds of cells:

  • Body cells: skin, lung, liver, muscle, blood, and so on.
  • Sex cells: eggs and sperm (and the cells that make them).

Only a mutation in a sex cell can be passed to children. If an egg or sperm carrying a mutation is part of fertilization, the mutation is copied into every cell of the child.

A mutation in a body cell affects only that person. For example, years of sun can cause mutations in skin cells that may lead to skin cancer, but the person's children do not inherit those mutations.

check.prompt: Which two mutations could be passed on to a person's children? Select two answers.
options: A mutation in a cell in the ovary that will become an egg
A mutation in a sperm cell that fertilizes an egg
A mutation in a skin cell caused by years of sunburns
A mutation in a lung cell caused by tobacco smoke
A mutation in a liver cell that occurred as the cell divided
why: Skin cells are body cells. The mutation may affect this person, but it is not in any egg or sperm, so children cannot inherit it.
Lung cells are body cells. Smoke can cause harmful mutations there, but they are not passed to children.
Liver cells are body cells. A copying error in a liver cell stays in that person's liver.
check.hint: Only egg and sperm cells (and the cells that make them) pass DNA to children.
check.explain: The cell that will become an egg and the sperm cell are sex cells, so their mutations can be inherited. The skin, lung, and liver mutations are in body cells; they can affect the person but are not passed on.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• DNA pairs A–T and C–G. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. A chromosome is a long DNA molecule with many genes. Humans: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); egg and sperm: 23.
  • Alleles are versions of a gene. Dominant (capital) shows if present; recessive (lowercase) needs two copies.
  • Genotype = letters; phenotype = trait seen. Homozygous = same; heterozygous = different. Carrier = heterozygous for a recessive disorder.
  • Punnett square: each box = 1/4 = 25%. Expected number = probability × total. Every child is a new event.

stimuli.title: Flower Color in Pea Plants
stimuli.html:
Pea plants have been used to study heredity for more than 150 years because they grow quickly, produce many seeds, and show traits that are easy to see. In pea plants, one gene controls flower color. The gene has two alleles: the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant, and the allele for white flowers (p) is recessive.

A plant breeder keeps three kinds of plants:

The breeder transfers pollen from one plant to another by hand so that she knows exactly which two plants are the parents of each batch of seeds. She then grows the seeds and records the flower color of each offspring plant.

stimuli.title: A Single Change in a Gene
stimuli.html:
Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The instructions for one part of hemoglobin are found in a gene on chromosome 11. In most people, one three-base group in this gene reads GAG. In the sickle cell allele, the middle base has been replaced, so the group reads GTG instead. This single change causes one amino acid in the protein to be different.

That small difference matters. When oxygen levels are low, the changed hemoglobin molecules stick together into long fibers. The fibers bend red blood cells into a stiff, curved “sickle” shape. Sickled cells can block small blood vessels, causing pain and organ damage, and they break down faster than normal cells.

The sickle cell allele is recessive for the disease. A person with two copies of the allele has sickle cell disease. A person with one copy is a carrier. Carriers usually have no symptoms, and studies have shown that carriers are less likely to become seriously ill from malaria, a disease spread by mosquitoes in parts of Africa, Asia, and South America. This protection helps explain why the allele is more common in regions where malaria has long been widespread.

stimuli.title: Cystic Fibrosis
stimuli.html:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an inherited disorder that affects the lungs and the digestive system. It is caused by changes in a gene on chromosome 7. This gene holds the instructions for a protein that forms a channel in the outer membrane of certain cells. The channel lets chloride, a part of salt, move in and out of the cell, which keeps the mucus on the cell's surface thin and slippery.

The most common CF allele is missing three bases from the gene. Because exactly three bases are missing, the rest of the gene is still read in the correct groups of three, but the protein is missing one amino acid (phenylalanine). That one missing amino acid causes the protein to fold into the wrong shape, and the cell breaks down most of it before it reaches the membrane. Without working channels, thick, sticky mucus builds up. It can clog the airways, trap bacteria that cause lung infections, and block the release of enzymes that digest food.

The CF allele is recessive. A person with two copies has cystic fibrosis. A person with one copy is a carrier and usually has no symptoms, so many carriers do not know they carry the allele. Today, many newborns are screened for CF with a blood test, and newer medicines that help the faulty protein work have improved the health of many patients.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship among DNA, genes, and chromosomes?
options: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule that contains many genes.

DNA is made of many chromosomes joined end to end.
A chromosome is a small section of one gene.
why: This reverses the relationship. Genes are sections of a chromosome, so a chromosome holds many genes, not the other way around.
Chromosomes are made of DNA, not the other way around. Each chromosome is one long DNA molecule.
This reverses the sizes. A gene is a small section of a chromosome; one chromosome holds many genes.
items.hint: Think of the size ladder: base, gene, chromosome.
items.explain:
A chromosome is one long, coiled DNA molecule, and a gene is a section of that DNA. So one chromosome carries many genes.

The groups after it shift: GCT TAC GAA becomes GTT ACG AA…. Every group after the deletion is different, so Mutation 2 is most likely to change the most amino acids.

items.prompt: Which mutation is most likely to cause the greatest change in the protein?
options: Mutation Z, because the added base shifts every group of three after it
Mutation Y, because it changes a group near the start of the gene
Mutation X, because it changes the very last base in the segment
None of them, because each version still begins with the group ATG
why: Mutation Y is a substitution (AAA → AGA). Being near the start does not matter; a substitution changes only its own group.
Mutation X is a substitution in the last group (TTT → TTC). It changes at most one group of three.
Keeping the first group the same does not protect the rest of the gene. Mutation Z changes every group after the insertion.
items.hint: Count the bases in each version. Which mutation changes the number of bases?

The groups after it shift: CCG TTT becomes ACC GTT T…. Because the insertion shifts every later group, Mutation Z is most likely to cause the greatest change.

items.prompt: A man develops skin cancer caused by mutations in his skin cells after many years of working in the sun. His adult daughter worries that she inherited these mutations from him. Which response is best supported by what you know about heredity?

She inherited them only if they arose before she was born, when he was younger.
why: A child receives DNA only through the egg and sperm. Mutations that arise in skin cells are not in his sperm, so they are not passed on.

Timing does not matter; location does. Even if the skin mutations happened before she was born, they were in skin cells, not sperm.

notes:
Study Notes: Genetics and Heredity

DNA Basics

  • Double helix; four bases.
  • A–T and C–G.
  • base < gene < chromosome < nucleus < cell
  • Gene = instructions for one protein.
  • Humans: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); egg and sperm: 23.

Punnett Square Steps

  1. Write both parent genotypes.
  2. One parent across the top, one down the side.
  3. Each box: one letter from top + one from side.
  4. Count: each box = 1/4 = 25%.

Expected number = probability × total

Ratio 3 : 1 means 3/4 and 1/4 (add the parts).

Work backward: 3 : 1 → Tt × Tt; 1 : 1 → Tt × tt; any recessive offspring → each parent carries the recessive allele. Each child is a new event.

Key Terms

  • Allele: one version of a gene.
  • Dominant (T) shows if present; recessive (t) needs two copies.
  • Genotype = letters; phenotype = trait seen.
  • Homozygous: TT or tt. Heterozygous: Tt.
  • Carrier: heterozygous for a recessive disorder.
  • Incomplete dominance: blend (RW = pink).
  • Codominance: both show (AB blood). Blood: multiple alleles (IA, IB, i; each person has two). IA, IB codominant; i (type O) recessive.

Mutations

  • Substitution: one base swapped.
  • Insertion: base added. Deletion: base removed (one base added or removed shifts every later group of three: frameshift; exactly three bases removed, as in the most common CF allele, removes one amino acid with no shift).
  • Causes: copying errors, UV light, X-rays, smoke, chemicals.
  • Harmful, neutral, or helpful.
  • Inherited only if in egg or sperm.
